newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW - Irish Permanent sees rosy 1997.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Irish Permanent sees rosy 1997.

text.p: Financial services group Irish Permanent Plc on Tuesday said its performance for the first month of 1997 was ahead of the same time last year and the fundamentals in the Irish housing market looked very promising.
"We have had a very good start to the year," chief executive Roy Douglas told Reuters after the release of 1996 results. "Our figures for January would be ahead of last year."
Irish Permanent reported an increase of 14.7 percent in pre-tax profit to 48.6 million Irish pounds in the year to December 31, 1996.
Douglas said he expects a very strong housing market in Ireland in 1997 but perhaps easing off from the levels of 1996.
Official figures show Ireland's house prices up 15 percent year-on-year to September 1996, and mortgage lending up 16.8 percent year-on-year to December 1996.
Irish Permanent, which has 90 percent of its total business in Ireland with 84 percent of that in residential mortgages, was a major beneficiary of the booming economy.
Douglas said new lending in residential mortgages was up 46 percent in 1996 and the group's market share had increased to 21 percent from 18 percent in 1995.

"Our market share did slip a bit in 1995 but we had a very strong focus on the market in 1996," Douglas said. "We have revamped our mortgage package, we had a much more competitive range of products, we dropped our fees and we have a very strong focus on the channel distribution business."
Douglas said Irish Permanent's balance sheet was also in very strong order and the group was on the lookout for new acquisitions, particularly in the Irish market.

"We are very focused on developing and growing our business and we would like to do that through acquisition if the suitable opportunity came along," he said. "We are very focused on Ireland to consolidate our position"
Douglas said Irish Permanent was particularly interested
in Ireland's TSB Bank which is governed by a board of trustees but whose main shareholder is the Irish government.
"As you know we are interested in the TSB if and when the
trustees and the minister might put it on the marketplace," he said. "The TSB has a very good branch network and would fit well with ours, particularly in the south of Ireland."
